data.title: Five questions before your first robot cell
data.excerpt: Material feed, fixturing, exceptions, and the person who recovers the cell at 2 a.m. decide whether a robot cell works.
data.body:
Robot cells fail for human reasons more often than mechanical ones. Before comparing payloads and reach, answer five questions about the work around the robot.

The five questions

  • How does material arrive, and how often is it out of specification?

  • What happens when the robot cannot pick the part?

  • Who recovers the cell, and how long does recovery take?

  • Which quality checks move into the cell, and which stay manual?

  • How will the cell be cleaned, maintained, and safely isolated?

Design the exception first

A cell that runs perfectly 95% of the time and stops the line for an hour in the other 5% is not a good investment. Put the exception path, the sensor strategy, and the recovery routine in the concept design, not the commissioning checklist.

The most successful first cells are usually narrow, well-bounded, and supported by a team that was involved from the start.
